en.title: Clauses of condition
en.summary: A clause of condition begins with if or unless.

paragraphs: A clause of condition says under what circumstances the main clause is true. It begins with if or with a word of similar meaning, and the verb forms follow clear patterns that show how real or unreal the condition is.

items: **Provided that you pay**, you may enter.

blocks.html:
TypeIf-clauseMain clauseExample
general truthpresent simplepresent simpleIf you heat ice, it melts.
real futurepresent simplewill + baseIf it rains, I'll stay.
unreal presentpast simplewould + baseIf I were rich, I'd travel.
unreal pastpast perfectwould have + participleIf I had known, I'd have helped.

WordMeaningExample
unlessif... notUnless it stops, we'll stay.
provided / providing (that)only ifProvided that you pay, you may go.
as long asonly ifYou can borrow it as long as you return it.
in caseto be ready ifTake a coat in case it rains.
even ifwhether or notI'll go even if it rains.
otherwiseif not (between sentences)Hurry; otherwise, we'll be late.

paragraphs: In formal English, if can be left out by inverting the subject and the auxiliary: Had I known, I would have called (= If I had known). Should you need help, call me (= If you should need). Were he here, he would help (= If he were here).

items: Wrong: **If it will rain, we'll stay.** Right: **If it rains**
Wrong: **If I would have money, I'd buy it.** Right: **If I had money**
Wrong: **Unless you don't hurry, you'll be late.** Right: **Unless you hurry** (unless already means if... not)
